slides.title: Chapter 22: Reading Text from Images with OCR
slides.say: This chapter is about reading the text out of a picture, which is called optical character recognition, or OCR. It has fifteen examples, and all of them run on the chapter page in the order of this deck. The pictures are drawn by the examples themselves, so no file has to be downloaded. Part 1 installs the engine and reads a first line. Part 2 measures what makes a reading fail. Part 3 repairs pictures and names languages. Part 4 finds mistakes, writes a searchable PDF and calls a scanner program. Part 5 reads the screen and ends with the practice program. Slide 2 gives the route through the parts.

slides.title: Today's route through five parts
slides.say: The chapter has five parts. Part 1 explains the two pieces that OCR needs, the program Tesseract and the module pytesseract, and reads a line, several lines and single words. Part 2 measures three limits: the height of the text, the tilt of the page and the noise on the picture. Part 3 repairs pictures, narrows a reading with settings and reads German and French. Part 4 compares a reading with a known text, writes a PDF and calls NAPS2. Part 5 reads a region of the screen and loops over pages. Each range on the slide is a run of slides you can jump to. Slide 3 gives the two questions that the parts answer.

slides.title: Two questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Two questions frame the chapter. The first asks which properties of a picture decide whether Tesseract can read it, and how far each can go. Part 2 answers it with three measured limits, and the summary repeats them. The second asks how a program reads a region of the screen, keeps the text and notices when the reading went wrong. Part 4 gives the way to notice mistakes and part 5 gives the screen loop. The practice slide lets you check yourself on both questions. The answers come back on slide 37.

slides.title: Part 1: The engine and the first reading
slides.say: Part 1 starts with the two pieces that OCR needs. Tesseract is a separate program that does the reading, and pytesseract is a small Python module that hands it a picture and returns the text. The part then reads one line with image_to_string(), reads three lines and looks at the single str that comes back, and finally asks for every word with its position and its confidence. Slide 7 shows how to check that the engine is installed and which languages it knows.

slides.title: Installing Tesseract and pytesseract
slides.say: Reading text from a picture needs two parts. Tesseract is a program, installed with an installer on Windows and macOS or with the package manager on Linux. pytesseract is a Python module, installed with pip, which only sends the picture to Tesseract and returns the answer. If the program is missing, the module raises an error. get_languages() lists the language files that are installed, and English is always among them. The book also uses the NAPS2 scanner, which needs its own English data. Slide 7 shows the version and the language list.

slides.title: Story: A machine of 1931 searched microfilm by recognizing patterns
slides.say: In 1931 the engineer Emanuel Goldberg was granted US patent 1,838,389 for his Statistical Machine. It searched rolls of microfilm with photoelectric cells and pattern recognition, so it matched shapes without a person reading them. The picture shows the memorial stone laid for him in Dresden, which gives his birth year, 1881, his flight in 1933 to France and his move in 1937 to Palestine. The idea of finding the shapes of characters by machine is the same as that of Tesseract. Slide 7 shows how the engine is called from Python.

slides.title: Is the engine installed, and which languages does it know?
slides.say: The first printed line is the version of Tesseract that ran, 5.3.4. The second line says that 22 language files are installed and shows the first five: ara, chi_sim, chi_tra, deu and eng. The last line is True for eng and False for xyz, which means the English file is installed and a file named xyz is not. pytesseract does not read anything itself: it starts the program Tesseract, so a missing program is the first thing to check when a reading fails. Slide 24 uses deu and fra from the same list.

slides.title: OCR fundamentals and the first reading
slides.say: Optical character recognition turns a picture of text into text. In pytesseract the central call is image_to_string(), which takes a picture, either an Image object made by Pillow or one opened with Image.open(), and returns everything that was read as a single str. The book uses a four-line picture, ocr-example.png, and a scan of a printed page from an 1831 print of Frankenstein, shown as its Figure 22-1. The next slides read pictures that the examples draw themselves, so they need no download. Slide 9 reads the first line.

slides.title: Reading one line with image_to_string()
slides.say: The printed result is 'Hello OCR 2026' followed by a line break, and the second line says True: after strip() the text equals the sentence that was drawn. The picture is drawn by the example, black text on a white ground, 440 by 90 pixels, with the font that Pillow itself carries. image_to_string() returns a str, and Tesseract always ends it with a line break, so strip() is the usual second step. Reading clear text in a large size is the easy case; the next examples make it harder. Slide 10 reads several lines in one call.

slides.title: Lines, line breaks and the answer's type
slides.say: The picture has three lines, and image_to_string() returned one str of 83 characters for all of them. splitlines() shows what was read: the second line contains a vertical bar where the word 'I' stood, so Tesseract made a mistake even on clean text, and an empty string appears between the second and the third line, which is the blank line that Tesseract inserts. A program that uses the text must expect both. Part 4 shows how to find such mistakes by comparing with the truth. Compare slide 11, which asks for each word and its position.

slides.title: Words with boxes and confidence: image_to_data()
slides.say: image_to_data() returns, for the same line, a dictionary of lists: the word, its confidence and its position. The four words are Invoice, 2026-114, total and 482.50, each with a confidence of 96 out of 100, and the left and top numbers show where each word stands: 23, 133, 281 and 352 pixels from the left. Empty entries, which stand for lines and blocks, are skipped with strip(). A program can use the confidence to decide which words to check by hand, and the position to crop a word. See slide 28 for the use of such results in finding mistakes.

slides.title: Part 2: What makes reading fail
slides.say: Part 2 asks what makes a reading fail. A program that reads text from pictures is only useful if you know where it stops working, so each example changes one property of the same sentence and prints a score from 0 to 1. The properties are the height of the text, the tilt of the page and the noise on the picture. The comparison table on slide 18 collects the three limits that the runs found, together with the repairs that part 3 tests.

slides.title: Preparing a picture for reading
slides.say: Preprocessing means changing a picture before it is read, so that the reading improves. The usual changes are turning a tilted page back, enlarging text that is too small, removing noise and reducing the picture to black and white. Not every change helps: the examples of part 2 first find where a reading fails, and the first example of part 3 tests two repairs and one that made a reading worse. Each change should be tested on the same picture and compared by a score. Slide 18 collects the limits.

slides.title: Story: The first reading machine for blind people was unveiled in 1976
slides.say: Ray Kurzweil founded Kurzweil Computer Products in 1974 to build OCR that could read any typeface and not only one fixed font. The reading machine for blind people, which scanned a page and read it aloud, was unveiled on 13 January 1976. The story belongs before part 2 because such a machine also needed a good picture: the next slides measure how small, how crooked and how noisy a picture may be before Tesseract fails.

slides.title: How small can the text be?
slides.say: The loop prints a score for each text height. At 7 and 8 pixels the reading is empty and the score is 0.0; at 9 pixels it is 0.95; at 10 pixels it is 0.99; and from 12 pixels it is 1.0. The score is the similarity of the reading to the sentence that was drawn, from difflib. A text smaller than about 9 pixels cannot be read, which is why scans are made at a high resolution. The repair, enlarging the picture, is tested in part 3. Compare slides 16 and 17, which change the tilt and the noise instead.

slides.title: How crooked can the page be?
slides.say: The same sentence is turned by an angle. At 0 and 4 degrees the score is 1.0, at 6 degrees 0.98, at 7 degrees 0.9, at 8 degrees 0.91, and at 9 and 12 degrees the reading is empty or wrong: 0.0 and 0.25. A page that is scanned crookedly by less than about 8 degrees is still read, and a page tilted more must be turned back first. The first example of part 3 turns a picture back and measures the gain. See slide 22 for the repair.

slides.title: How much noise can the picture carry?
slides.say: NumPy adds a random value between minus s and plus s to every pixel, and the loop prints the score for six values of s. Up to 100 the score is 1.0; at 105 and above the reading is empty. The change is abrupt: the text is read perfectly or not at all, so a program should check its result and not rely on the noise being small. The noise here is uniform random noise; a scan has other kinds, such as stains, and they need other repairs. Compare slide 15 and slide 16; slide 18 puts the three limits together.

slides.title: Three limits of a reading, measured by the run
slides.say: The table collects the three limits that the runs of this part measured and the repairs that were tested. The text must be at least 9 pixels high, the page may be tilted up to 8 degrees, and the noise may reach 100. A tilted page is repaired completely by turning it back, small text is repaired by enlarging it three times, and no repair for noise was found in these examples. Every number in the table was measured by the program when this deck was built, with Tesseract 5.3.4 and one font. See slides 15, 16 and 17 for the runs behind the numbers.

slides.title: Part 3: Cleaning, settings and languages
slides.say: Part 3 repairs and steers a reading. The first example turns a tilted picture back and enlarges a small one, and it also shows that reducing a picture to black and white can make a reading worse, so every step needs a test. The second example gives Tesseract settings: a page mode that says one line, and a whitelist of the characters that may appear. The third reads German and French with the language files that name them, and shows the error of a language that is not installed.

slides.title: Languages other than English
slides.say: Tesseract reads English unless it is told otherwise. For another language you install its language file and pass the code with lang=, for example lang='deu' for German. Two files can be joined with a plus sign, as in lang='eng+jpn'. The book's example reads a page with Japanese text, frankenstein_jpn.png. With only the English file, an accented letter is read as another letter, and a language that is not installed raises an error. Slide 24 shows both results.

slides.title: Story: Tesseract began at Hewlett-Packard in 1985 and became open source
slides.say: Tesseract was developed at Hewlett-Packard laboratories from 1985. Hewlett-Packard released it as open source in 2005, and Google sponsored its development from 2006. Because it is open source, other tools can offer it: the picture shows the transcription tool of Wikisource, where Tesseract OCR is one choice, set here to the Tamil script, and pytesseract does the same calling for Python. The slides that follow use version 5.3.4, and the language files that come with it, to read English, German and French. See also slide 7, where the version is printed.

slides.title: Cleaning a picture before reading it
slides.say: Three printed lines show three repairs. A page tilted by 10 degrees scores 0.0, and turned back by 10 degrees it scores 1.0. A text of 8 pixels scores 0.0, and enlarged three times with the LANCZOS filter it scores 0.98. The last line applies a black-and-white table with point() to the enlarged picture and the score falls to 0.7, so that step made the reading worse. A repair must be tested on the picture at hand; a step that helps one picture can hurt another. See slide 18 for the limits that these repairs address.

slides.title: Page modes and a whitelist of characters
slides.say: The first line is the reading without settings: Call 555-0199 now: 2026. The second line uses two settings in one string: --psm 7 tells Tesseract that the picture holds a single line, and tessedit_char_whitelist lists the only characters that may be returned. The result is 555-01992026, digits and the hyphen only, and the spaces and letters are gone. Settings are passed in the config argument. A whitelist suits fields such as telephone numbers, and it also makes a reading wrong when the field holds other characters.

slides.title: Reading German and French with lang=
slides.say: The same picture is read twice, once as English and once as its own language. For the German line the similarity to the truth rises from 0.83 to 1.0 with lang='deu', and for the French line from 0.86 to 1.0 with lang='fra'. The English file has no letters such as ü, ß or é, so it replaces them with similar ones. The last line shows that asking for a language that is not installed raises a TesseractError. The font DejaVu Sans is used because the font of Pillow has no accented letters. Slide 20 explains the language files.

slides.title: Part 4: Mistakes, PDF and scanners
slides.say: Part 4 is about what comes after a reading. A reading has mistakes, so the first example compares it with a known text and lists each difference, which is also the first step of any automatic correction, including one done by a language model. The second example writes a PDF whose invisible text layer can be searched. The third calls the scanner program NAPS2 from Python with subprocess, and shows what Python does when that program is not installed.

slides.title: Mistakes, searchable PDFs and NAPS2
slides.say: Three ideas of this part belong together. A reading has mistakes, and a language model can correct what remains, but the program must still check the correction against the source. NAPS2 is a free scanner program with a command line, and subprocess.run() starts any program with a list of arguments; check=True raises an error when the program fails. The arguments -i and -o name the input picture and the output file, and -n 0 scans no new page. OCRmyPDF is another program that adds an invisible text layer to a PDF. Slides 28, 29 and 30 hold the three examples.

slides.title: Story: reCAPTCHA used what OCR could not read to digitize books
slides.say: reCAPTCHA began at Carnegie Mellon University in a team around Luis von Ahn, and Google acquired it in September 2009. A visitor was shown two words: one that the program already knew and one that OCR had not been able to read. A correct answer to the known word gave weight to the answer for the other one, and the answers digitized books. The comparison with a known text is the idea of the next slides, which find the mistakes of a reading. Compare slide 28, which finds the mistakes of a reading.

slides.title: Finding the mistakes of a reading
slides.say: The example uses a reading with four typical mistakes: a lower-case l for a capital I, a capital O for a zero, a capital I for a lower-case l, and another O for a zero. get_opcodes() lists each place where the two texts differ, and the loop prints the true character and what was read. The last line is the similarity, 0.86. A program can use such a list to decide what to correct, whether by hand, by a rule or by a language model; the corrected text should be compared with the source again.

slides.title: A searchable PDF from a picture
slides.say: image_to_pdf_or_hocr() returns bytes, and they start with %PDF-, so the result is a PDF. It contains the picture and an invisible layer of the text that was read. The example writes the bytes to a file and starts pdftotext, another program, with subprocess.run(); the list it prints holds both lines of the page, so the text of the picture can be searched and copied. The extension argument can also be 'hocr' for a web page that keeps the position of every word.

slides.title: Running the scanner program NAPS2 from Python
slides.say: The first line prints the command as one string: NAPS2.Console -n 0 -i ocr-example.png -o output.pdf. The arguments are given to subprocess.run() as a list, one word each. NAPS2 is not installed on the machine that ran this example, so Python raises FileNotFoundError and the program prints its name and the missing file name, NAPS2.Console. The try statement turns a missing program into a message; with check=True a program that starts and fails raises a different error, CalledProcessError. Compare slide 29, which starts pdftotext in the same way.

slides.title: Part 5: The screen and the practice program
slides.say: Part 5 reads the screen. A screenshot is a picture, so everything of the earlier parts applies to it: crop it to the text, read it and keep the result. The first example uses an emulated screen, because the real screenshot function needs a display. The second example is the practice program of the chapter, a browser text scraper: for each page of a document it takes a screenshot, crops it, reads it and appends the text to a file. The questions after it let you check the whole chapter.

slides.title: The screen and the practice program
slides.say: pyautogui is a third-party module that controls the mouse, the keyboard and the screen. Its screenshot() function returns a picture of the screen as an Image, which can be cropped and read like any other picture. The book's Figure 22-2 shows a web page with an embedded document whose text cannot be copied, which is the case for the practice program, the browser text scraper. It reads each page of the document from a screenshot and appends the text to output.txt; the book's program is called ocrscreen.py. Slide 36 has the questions.

slides.title: Story: The 1831 edition of Frankenstein is the page the book scans
slides.say: Mary Shelley's Frankenstein appeared anonymously in 1818, and a revised edition of 1831 carries her name. The picture is the frontispiece engraving of that edition, made by Theodor von Holst and now in the public domain. The book's Figure 22-1 is a scan of a page of the same print, a hard case for OCR because of the age of the paper and the typeface. The screenshot of the next slides is the easy case, since screen text is sharp. See also slide 34, where a screenshot is read.

slides.title: Reading text from the screen
slides.say: The example draws its own screen, because the real screenshot function of pyautogui needs a display, and it says EMULATED. The screenshot is 640 by 300 pixels, and the crop keeps the region from row 50 to row 170, 640 by 120 pixels. Tesseract reads only that region and returns the lines Embedded document and Page 3 of 12: total 482.50 with an empty string between them. Cropping first removes the browser bar and everything else that is not text, which makes the reading faster and cleaner. See slide 35 for the loop that repeats it.

slides.title: Practice program: a browser text scraper
slides.say: The practice program of the chapter is a browser text scraper. The example draws three emulated pages of a document. For each page the loop takes a screenshot, crops it, reads it and appends the text and a line break to output.txt. The last line prints the file's three lines: Page 1 of 3: total 100.50, Page 2 of 3: total 200.50 and Page 3 of 3: total 300.50. In the book the pages are changed by pressing a key, which needs a display; the loop is the same. Compare slide 34, which reads one screenshot.

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: These are the practice questions, and each points to the part where the idea was shown. The first is about the two installed parts and get_languages(), slide 7. The second is about the smallest text height that reads well, slide 15. The third is about the whitelist, slide 23. The fourth is about languages and the error of a missing one, slide 24. The fifth is about the scraper's loop, slide 35. Run the examples on the chapter page to check each answer.

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Four sentences carry the chapter. pytesseract is a bridge to the program Tesseract, and image_to_string() returns a str. Size, tilt and noise each have a limit, and turning a page back and enlarging small text are repairs that work. lang= names the language, and the settings --psm and a whitelist narrow a reading. A reading should be compared with a known text, and a screenshot should be cropped to its text before it is read. Slides 3 and 36 give the two questions and the practice questions again.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: These fifteen links are where to go next. They include the chapter of the book, the documentation of Tesseract, pytesseract, NAPS2, OCRmyPDF and PyAutoGUI, the Python documentation for difflib and subprocess, and the pages behind the stories: Emanuel Goldberg, Kurzweil Computer Products, Tesseract, reCAPTCHA and Frankenstein. Each page shows the date on which it was opened. Use the documentation pages to find options that the examples do not use, such as other page modes. See also slide 3 for the two questions of the chapter.
